RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture. SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is mildly an opportunity, not a crisis. The dispute is still in the investigation-and-signaling phase: the August 2017 Section 301 opening, a November Beijing visit that produced large announced deals but “no substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer,” and the January 22 Section 201 safeguards as the first real tariff shot. Escalating without the 301 record, or conceding for more MOUs, both waste the present advantage.

USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with a calibrated Section 301 tariff package aimed at Chinese industrial-policy and technology goods (the $30–60 billion range already under White House debate), not another global metals-style blast. Pair the announcement with a clear offer of talks on forced technology transfer, JV/equity caps, and discriminatory licensing, and keep investment restrictions and visa measures in reserve until they are legally tight. Do not roll back the newly signed 232 steel/aluminum duties yet, but stop widening them and use ally exemptions to rebuild a coalition for the China IP case.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is an opportunity, not an emergency. The underlying Chinese practices are real and costly — USTR’s 301 inquiry (opened after the 14 Aug 2017 memorandum) targets JV/equity-forced transfer, non-market licensing, state-directed acquisition of U.S. tech, and cyber-enabled IP theft; USCBC’s Sep 2017 filing said nearly 20% of member firms had been asked to transfer technology in three years, and Lighthizer has flagged Made in China 2025 as the industrial-policy core. The 8 Nov 2017 Beijing visit produced commercial MOUs and no structural IP concessions; China rejected 301 consultations as “irresponsible.” That is a genuine long-run threat to U.S. tech leadership, but it is not yet an existential or even high near-term shock: U.S. consumer sentiment is 101.4 (Mar 2018), industrial production is rising (102.2), CPI is contained, the goods deficit is large but not newly crisis-like (~$69.8bn in Mar), and VIX has settled near 18 after the February spike. China remains more goods-export exposed to the U.S. (U.S. imports from China still ~$38bn/month vs ~$12.7bn exports) with stable reserves (~$3.16tn) and a stronger yuan (~6.32), so the terrain favors using leverage.

Action should therefore be moderate escalation on the right instrument, not hold and not maximal war. Steel/aluminum 232 (signed 8 Mar) is the wrong lead tool against Beijing — China is only ~2% of U.S. steel imports after existing AD/CVD, while Canada, Brazil, Korea, Japan and the EU absorb the hit and have already threatened WTO cases and retaliation. Stacking an unfocused China package on top of that ally backlash would waste the one issue (IP/tech transfer) that has bipartisan and business support. A targeted 301 tariff list aimed at MIC 2025 products is the proportionate use of leverage after seven months of a completed investigation and a failed summit. Restraint below maximal escalation is required because China has already previewed farm-belt counters (sorghum AD/CVD after the Jan Section 201 solar/washer tariffs; ASA reports Beijing named soybeans — $12–14bn of U.S. exports — as a prime target, with Brazil as a ready substitute) and Lighthizer himself told Ways & Means on 21 Mar that Chinese retaliation is “inevitable.” Concede-purchases or rollback would cash in unused leverage for nothing; hold would ratify Beijing’s bet that Washington will blink. Calibrated 301 tariffs plus an open negotiating door is the action that matches a mild opportunity reading.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Answer the already-signed Section 232 metals tariffs with a tightly scoped, WTO-framed counter-list (U.S. farm and other politically salient goods sized to China's actual 232 exposure) and file at the WTO, while keeping a larger 301 response list ready but unpublished until Washington names products and dollar amounts. Do not pre-emptively launch a broad tariff war, do not offer purchase or structural concessions before a 301 package exists, and keep Liu He’s channel open so talks can resume once the U.S. list is public. Use the fact that 232 also hits EU, Japan and Korea to isolate Washington's method, not to concede on JV, licensing or Made-in-China industrial policy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not yet high in the CHN-anchor sense. The live measures—Section 201 solar/washer safeguards and global 25%/10% Section 232 metals tariffs signed 8 March, effective 23 March—are hostile and were announced while Liu He was still in Washington, and Trump has framed the dispute as a trade war he thinks is “good, and easy to win.” Direct 232 damage to China is small: China is only ~2% of U.S. steel imports and ~0.1% of Chinese steel output, and ships little raw aluminum to the U.S., so this is not a major-export-sector shock. The larger threat is the imminent Section 301 package: as of 21 March the White House said the President would announce 301 actions the next day, with reporting of $30–60bn of China-specific tariffs aimed at forced tech transfer, JV/equity limits, outbound tech acquisitions and cyber-enabled IP theft—i.e., the industrial-policy core, not just metals. That is why threat sits near +0.32, not 0 and not +0.5: the target is strategic, bipartisan in Washington, and Lighthizer has already said Chinese retaliation (especially on agriculture) is expected and will not deter the U.S. Macro data do not yet show the dispute biting: industrial production still ~6% y/y, reserves ~$3.16tn and rising, merchandise exports still large, discount rate unchanged at 2.9%, and CNY stronger (about 6.32 vs ~6.62 six months earlier)—no FX or financial-stability stress. Action should therefore be retaliate, not hold and not concede: a proportional 232 reply defends legitimacy and domestic industry associations that have already demanded counters, while a maximal tariff/entity-list escalation before the 301 list is public would waste the ally-alienation created by global 232, play into Trump’s shock-value strategy, and risk a spiral China does not need while the real economy is still healthy. Purchase or structural concessions are inappropriate: November’s Beijing commercial MOUs bought no IP relief, Liu He’s late-February talks did not stop 232, and there is no matching U.S. offer on the table.

RECOMMENDATION: Hold the published Section 301 $50 billion list in place as bargaining leverage, do not implement it during the open comment window, and do not proceed now with the additional $100 billion consideration. Prepare a USDA contingency for farmers already hit by the April 2 pork/fruit duties, but do not expand tariffs until talks have a chance to convert the 301 findings into concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is modestly positive, not existential. USTR’s March 22 Section 301 report documented unreasonable IP and tech-transfer practices and estimated at least $50 billion of annual U.S. harm; the November 2017 Beijing visit produced commercial MOUs but no structural IP concessions, so the underlying problem is real. The current dispute state has begun to impose costs on the United States before any remedy is in hand: China implemented ~$3 billion of Section 232 retaliation on April 2 (pork, fruit, nuts, wine), then on April 4 proposed a matching 25% list on ~$50 billion including soybeans (~$14 billion of U.S. exports), autos, and aircraft, timed to hit the farm belt. Farm groups called that “devastating,” and VIX remains elevated near 20 after the March 22–April 4 sequence. That is not yet a material GDP event: U.S. industrial production is still rising, Michigan sentiment is 98.8, and CPI is contained. China’s industrial output and reserves (~$3.14 trillion) are also stable, so Beijing is not overextended. Net: some farm-sector and political exposure, plus an unremedied IP problem, against still-strong U.S. macro and unused tariff leverage — hence +0.15, well below the +0.5 “material GDP drag” anchor.

The action stance is hold-and-talk, not further escalate. The $50 billion 301 list is still only proposed (comments due May 11, hearing May 15); China’s $50 billion list is likewise not in force and Vice Finance Minister Zhu said timing depends on negotiations. Mnuchin has acknowledged “the potential of a trade war” while saying talks continue; Kudlow and Navarro say the process can still be resolved. Adding another $100 billion now, as instructed on April 5, would push the fight into consumer goods, likely lock in China’s soy/aircraft list, and rattle markets further (Dow futures sold off on that announcement) without a finished Chinese offer on the table. Rolling back or offering purchase commitments would surrender leverage before Beijing has moved on IP. Negotiate from the existing 301 list and the parallel WTO licensing case; convert the comment window into a structured negotiation rather than a second tariff round.

Ross–Liu talks (2–3 Jun) reproduced that pattern: a reported ~$70B ag/energy/manufacturing buy if Washington drops tariffs, with Beijing stating that any outcomes die if the U.S. proceeds. Implementing the teed-up $50B is therefore the proportionate next step — it converts the May 29 commitment into a credible bargaining chip rather than another bluff, and it is still far short of maximal escalation. That is why the threat reading is negative (opportunity/leverage) rather than zero: the US has unused, legitimate pressure on an issue with broader domestic buy-in than steel/aluminum. Action is moderate escalation, not maximal, because second-order risks are already visible. Section 232 steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) proclamations of 1–8 March are global, China is a small direct metals supplier, and Beijing has been cautious on 232 while warning that a China-specific follow-on will draw a justified and necessary response, with soybeans, aircraft, coal, and other politically resonant exports already named. Holding or rolling back would ratify the post-Beijing status quo; going maximal would turn a leverage opportunity into a farm-belt and ally-cohesion problem before talks have even been tested against a real tariff. Intended numeric stance: threat about minus zero point three (mild opportunity); action about minus zero point four five (moderate tariff escalation).

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a mild opportunity, not a danger, because the United States still holds the initiative and the real economy is not yet paying a material price. The Section 301 record (2017-08-14 investigation; 2018-03-22 findings and memorandum; 2018-04-03 proposed list of about 1300 lines / $50B aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and machinery) documents unresolved IP and Made-in-China-2025 practices after the November 2017 Beijing visit produced only commercial MOUs and no structural concessions. The offsetting costs that keep the score near zero rather than a large opportunity are real and already visible. On 2018-04-02 China implemented about $3B of 232 retaliation (pork, fruit, nuts, wine). On 2018-04-04 it proposed 25 percent duties on about $50B of US goods, ranking soybeans first (about $12–14B; about one-third of the US crop; about 40 percent of China soybean imports), plus autos and some aircraft, and said timing depends on what Washington does. Soy futures fell 3 to 5 percent the day of the announcement; the American Soybean Association put one-morning mark-to-market losses near $1.72B and called the hit devastating. Farm-state Republicans (Ernst, Fischer, Bacon) and USDA Perdue immediately flagged political and income risk in a sector already facing weak farm income. VIX remains about 20 (about double last fall) and jumped above 23 around the 301 rollout. Those are concentrated export and political threats, not a GDP or financial-stability event.

That combination justifies negotiate at action_score 0, not further tariff escalation and not rollback. Further escalation (the April 5 instruction to study another $100B) would likely bring implementation of China soy list, deepen farm-belt losses, and raise input-cost risk on the US 301 machinery/ICT lines before comments close (written comments to May 11; hearing May 15). Mnuchin and Kudlow have already described parallel talks (deficit cut on the order of $100B, end forced JVs/tech transfer) and Chinese Vice Finance Minister Zhu publicly asked Washington to work in a constructive manner while warning Beijing will not simply back down. Hold the published $50B list, keep the WTO licensing case, and bargain in the comment window.

RECOMMENDATION: Use the Trump-Xi G20 dinner to open a time-bound negotiation, not to settle. Hold the existing $250B tariff architecture in place and make any delay of the January 1 List 3 hike to 25% contingent on a short, enforceable work plan covering IP/tech transfer, not another purchase-pledge communiqué. Do not add the threatened ~$267B list this week, and do not roll back or lock in purchase commitments until China puts dates and verification on structural changes.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modest, not existential. The Section 301 case remains live—USTR’s March finding on IP/forced tech transfer, Lists 1–3 now covering ~$250B, and Lighthizer’s late-November assessment that China “has not fundamentally altered” those practices. That is a real interest at stake, but the US macro core is still intact: industrial production is slightly higher, Michigan sentiment is 97.5, and CPI is contained. The bite is concentrated and political: US goods exports to China fell ~15% from July to November (EXPCH $10.15B → $8.65B); soybean sales to China are down ~94% on 25% Chinese retaliation, with storage overflow and only a fraction of the $12B farm-aid package paid out; VIX is ~18.5 versus ~12 in June; the dollar is firmer and CNY has weakened to ~6.95. Those are farm-belt and market-volatility costs, not a recession. China is under more cyclical pressure (IP y/y 6.0 → 5.4, reserves down ~$56B, import compression), which is leverage, not a reason to declare victory. Action should stay near zero because the May 19 “trade war on hold” joint statement collapsed ten days later when Washington judged purchase language insufficient, and China’s recent 142-point list is again being read in Washington as thin on timetable and enforcement. Escalating into the G20 (auto-hiking List 3 or launching List 4) would hit more consumer-facing imports, invite broader Chinese retaliation against remaining US export channels, and waste the first leader-level opening since the November 1 call. Unconditional rollback or purchase concessions would repeat May and spend the January 1 deadline for another unenforceable truce. Negotiate: explore a pause of the scheduled hike only against a dated, verifiable structural track, and keep tariffs as the backstop if talks fail.

RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 90-day window to negotiate hard for enforceable structural commitments (IP, forced tech transfer, cyber, non-tariff barriers) plus immediate, measurable farm and energy purchases—without rolling back existing Section 301 tariffs or trading the Meng extradition case. Keep the suspended List 3 hike to 25% as the deadline incentive; do not add new tariff or entity-list actions while talks are live. Compartment the Huawei/Meng sanctions case from the trade table, and press Beijing to release the detained Canadians so the truce is not poisoned by hostage diplomacy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high: US industrial production is still firm (INDPRO ~104.1) and Michigan sentiment remains elevated at 98.3, so this is not a recession-scale shock. The bite is concentrated and political—US goods exports to China are down ~9% in the lookback, China’s matching retaliation on soy/autos/aircraft has already cratered farm-belt demand (US soybean sales to China down ~94% through mid-October; Illinois soy prices fell ~$2.50/bu), and USDA had to stand up a $12B aid package. Markets are signaling risk (VIX 25.58 on 19 Dec, +48% in-window; 10-year yield back to 2.77 from a 3.24 peak; WTI −31%). The Dec 1 G20 pause bought time by freezing the Jan 1 List 3 hike, but there is no joint text: Washington claims a 90-day structural clock and “very substantial” immediate purchases; Beijing describes only a halt to new tariffs and gradual import increases “according to domestic needs.” Same-day arrest of Meng Wanzhou on a US Iran-sanctions warrant, followed by China’s Dec 10 detention of Kovrig and Spavor, injects a second track that could collapse talks if either side escalates. That mix is a modest threat (+0.22), not an opportunity to restructure on US terms and not an existential cascade. Action should therefore stay near zero: negotiate inside the window rather than escalate (which would hit already-stressed markets and farm constituencies) or concede (existing $250B of 301 coverage is the leverage, and China has not yet delivered matching structural offers). Second-order risk of further tariff hikes now is a Chinese walk-away plus deeper soy-market diversion to Brazil; second-order risk of premature rollback is losing the only instrument that brought Xi to the table.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the G20 90-day window open and treat the January high-level talks as a purchase-and-process negotiation, not a structural surrender. Offer a large, verifiable increase in US agricultural, energy, and manufactured-goods imports to give Washington a face-saving path to leave List 3 at 10% past the March deadline, while refusing irreversible changes to industrial policy, SOE governance, or Made-in-China 2025. Do not add tariffs or further high-profile detentions during the truce; those would likely collapse talks and trigger the already-scheduled 10-to-25% hike on ~$200B of Chinese exports.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. Combined US Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (Lists 1–3), China’s matching retaliation tops out around $60B plus the earlier $3B 232 package, and the Jan 1, 2019 List-3 hike to 25% is only suspended—not cancelled—pending a deal (timeline 2018-09-24, 2018-12-01). Firm-level targeting is real and escalating: the April 2018 ZTE denial order, Meng Wanzhou’s 1 Dec arrest, the 10 Dec detention of Kovrig and Spavor, and the 28 Jan DOJ fraud/sanctions/trade-secret charges plus formal extradition request all hit a national-champion tech champion (timeline 2018-04-16, 2018-12-01, 2018-12-10, 2019-01-28). Official 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% and Q4 to 6.4%—a three-decade low—with December exports contracting as tariffs began to bite, auto sales weak, and NBS acknowledging rising downward pressure. That maps near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export sectors, Huawei, unemployment risk in export hubs) but not +1.0: industrial production was still +5.7% y/y in December, FX reserves held ~$3.11T, the yuan strengthened from ~6.97 in late October to 6.71 on 30 Jan, and high-level talks are live (Lighthizer/Mnuchin, 30 Jan) with purchase commitments on the table and structural IP/tech-transfer still unresolved (timeline 2019-01-07, 2019-01-30). Action should stay near zero because a May-2018 purchases-only truce already collapsed when the White House reopened 301, Lighthizer is publicly demanding verification and structural change rather than another empty soybean pledge, and further Chinese escalation (new tariffs or more hostage diplomacy) would give hawks the pretext to let the March hike proceed. Negotiation—purchases plus process, no core concession—is the stance that uses US market-sensitivity (UMCSENT 91.2, US goods exports to China down ~27% in the window) without trading away the industrial model the Party will not give up.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a mild US opportunity, not a high-cost emergency. The US already covers ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%) and still holds the unused 10%→25% hike as leverage; Beijing has come back to the table since the G20 truce and is offering larger purchases, while the White House and Xi both described the Feb 14–15 Beijing round as progress toward an MOU even as the official US readout said “much work remains” on structural issues. Escalating now would likely stall talks that Trump himself called “not a magical” March 1 deadline and would raise costs on the consumer-heavy List 3 just as companies are already rerouting supply chains. Rolling back without enforcement would repeat the May 19–29 2018 false truce, when purchase talk was followed by the White House restarting 301 actions. Negotiate: hold the current tariff stock, press for a verifiable enforcement snap-back, and only extend the hike if the text is close.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is mildly negative (slight U.S. opportunity) because the dispute is still in the U.S. initiative phase and is not yet imposing a GDP or export shock. The November 8, 2017 Beijing visit produced a large commercial-deal package that yielded no substantive concessions on those structural issues, which is why the current state is an opportunity to apply unused leverage rather than a crisis already damaging the U.S. economy. Action should stay near hold/negotiate because (1) firing 301 remedies before findings are issued would jump the legal process and hand Beijing a WTO/unilateralism talking point it has already previewed (MOFCOM “strong dissatisfaction,” Gao Feng warning of “all necessary measures”); (2) China’s reaction to the January 22 Section 201 solar/washer tariffs has so far been protest and a WTO posture, not a farm-belt retaliation cycle, so there is nothing to “retaliate” against and no case for concession; and (3) Commerce’s February 16 Section 232 options (24% global steel or 53% on a 12-country list including China; 7.7% global aluminum or 23.5% on China and others) are the higher-risk tool—allies and U.S. downstream users (autos, Business Roundtable) have already signaled retaliation and cost shocks, which would spend alliance capital the United States needs if 301 later requires a coalition. The disciplined move is therefore to negotiate under the shadow of a nearly complete 301 case, not to escalate tariffs now and not to give away 201 relief for another empty MOU.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but contained, not existential. U.S. farm exports have already taken a large hit—soybean shipments to China fell from $12.2B in 2017 to $3.1B in 2018, with a further ~44% drop in Jan–Sep 2019 vs 2018—and Washington has spent on the order of $28B in farm aid (Forbes/CNN Dec 6; Newsweek Dec 6). U.S. manufacturing is in its deepest slump in a decade, with ISM contracting into early December and survey respondents citing tariffs and global trade as the main cross-industry drag (Business Insider Dec 2; CBS/ISM Oct). List 4B would, for the first time, tax phones, laptops, toys and apparel just before Christmas—costs that fall on U.S. households and retailers, not only on Beijing (SCMP Nov 21; Reuters Dec 10). That is a material GDP-and-politics drag, but the consumer still holds and talks are on the doorstep, so the reading sits well below the +0.5 “high threat” anchor.

The same facts argue against both escalation and concession. After the May collapse (List 3 to 25%, Huawei Entity List, Chinese retaliation) and the August currency-manipulator designation, the Oct 11 Washington round produced a Phase One in principle: $40–50B annual U.S. farm purchases, IP and currency language, and a delay of the mid-October hike (timeline Oct 11; Politico Oct 11). China has since signaled goodwill with farm-tariff exemptions (timeline Sep 11–13; finance-ministry waivers Dec 6). Outstanding gaps as of Dec 10 are how to lock purchases and which existing tariffs to roll back—not whether a deal is conceivable (Bloomberg Dec 4; Economic Times/Bloomberg Dec 10). Sources close to both sides say neither wants 4B to land (SCMP Nov 21). Letting it fire would likely kill talks for the rest of the term (Reuters Dec 10) and invite Chinese retaliation into the 2020 cycle. Full or large rollback of the 25% lists would give away remaining leverage before structural issues are even on the table. Hong Kong legislation (signed late November) has already injected a separate political irritant; adding a consumer-tariff shock on top would compound risk without improving the bargain. Negotiate the remaining short strokes, bank Phase One, keep Lists 1–3.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is elevated but not existential. Existing US tariffs already cover the bulk of merchandise exports (List 3 at 25% from 10 May; List 4A at 15% from 1 September), Huawei and affiliates remain on the Entity List with only a narrow temporary license, and CNY’s break of 7 plus the August currency-manipulator designation showed FX and legitimacy pressure. Factory-hub pain is real: industrial production growth hit a 17-year low of 4.8% in July, and US-bound exports were reported down more than 12% year-to-date by October, with capacity leaking to Vietnam and Indonesia. That maps near the CHN +0.5 anchor (major export sectors hit, firm-level Huawei targeting, unemployment risk in export hubs). It is not +1.0: November official manufacturing PMI returned to 50.2 after six months of contraction, Caixin PMI printed 51.8, and Beijing still has fiscal/credit tools. The live incremental threat is List 4B on ~$156–160B of phones, laptops, toys and apparel on 15 December — the first hit to China’s highest-value consumer electronics chain and a catalyst for faster supply-chain exit.

Action should therefore de-escalate on the purchase axis, not escalate. Talks are advanced and a matching US offer is on the table: the mid-October hike on $250B was already delayed as part of the 11 October “Phase One” in-principle deal (China to buy roughly $40–50B of US farm goods; IP and currency cited), MOFCOM on 7 November said both sides had agreed to remove additional tariffs in phases, and early-December reporting had negotiators close on the size of tariff relief with US officials expecting a text before 15 December. Farm purchases are the cheapest concession available — China already signaled goodwill by exempting soybeans and pork from extra retaliation in mid-September, and African swine fever means the pork/soy demand is real. A purchase commitment can buy cancellation of List 4B and a limited 4A rollback without surrendering Made-in-China 2025, the Entity List fight, or Hong Kong. Escalating first would likely land List 4B, validate Trump’s “look for an alternative to China” order, and waste a window in which Washington also has reasons (farm belt, impeachment, 2020) to prefer a truce. Full rollback or structural legal rewrite is not on offer and should not be volunteered; Phase Two issues stay for later. If the US lets 15 December fire despite a purchase package, then and only then mirror with the already-scheduled Chinese tranche.
